To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have used genetic mapping to identify novel protective antigens in a livestock parasite and have validated the use of this approach for identification of antigens that may be protective against other apicomplexans.
we have identified a novel protective antigen (IMP-1) and a novel protective antigen homologous to a known protective antigen (AMA-1).
We have identified two novel protective antigens for E. maxima and have shown that they can be used as effective vaccines.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of effective anti-parasite sub-unit vaccines.
the development of a vaccine against Eimeria maxime, a parasite which infects the gut of chickens and causes coccidiosis.
the identification of antigens that can be used to develop sub-unit vaccines against the major apicomplexan pathogens of livestock.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the identification of AMA- 1 and IMP- 1 represents a substantial advance in our ability to understand the basis of protective immunity to eimerian infection and, by inference, other apicomplexans, and that the approach used in this study may have broad application to other parasite systems.
we have identified novel protective antigens for an apicomplexan protozoan parasite.
the genetic mapping and population fingerprinting approach described here provides a novel and effective strategy to identify protective antigensi in apicomplexan species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified the first protective antigens for Eimeria spp., and that the methodology that we have used to identify these antigens is applicable to other apicomplexans and other parasites.
we have developed a novel approach to identify novel protective antigens for apicomplexan diseases.
we identified a novel protective protein in Eimeria maxmia, a parasite that causes disease in chickens.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it provides a novel approach to identify novel antigens for apicomplexan sub-unit vaccines.
genetic mapping of a complex trait, in this case immunity to a pathogenic parasite, can be used to identify the genomic regions associated with that complex trait.
we have developed a new strategy to identify novel protective antigens.
